open_points.subject: Models M30–M34 release-table provenance and lifecycle
open_points.text: Like M22–M29 they are the shapes of rows of tables the data provider holds for the release (SPEC_STANDARD §6.10), not reference tables of the specification, which never reach the running service (§5, §15.2).
open_points.question: For each of M30–M34, who authors and mints the row values, from which exact provider artifact, and when are runtime row values constructed or delivered?
options: The data provider owns one named release constant per model and delivers its rows to generated code.
The specification owns the correspondences and the data provider merely stores generated copies.
Registry derives the rows from other vocabularies or rules instead of receiving table values.
open_points.default_guess: The data provider is authoritative and delivers one explicitly named release constant per model; rows exist as immutable values for the lifetime of that release.

open_points.subject: Model M30 — FormFieldRefusalKind
open_points.text: The release: the form refusal table the data provider holds.
open_points.question: Which product actions read FormFieldRefusalKind rows, and does Registry read the table directly or receive an already-resolved refusal kind from the data provider?
options: Every server-side form validation reads the table directly.
Only specified owner-interface form submissions read it.
The data provider resolves the refusal kind, so no Registry action reads the row model.
The table is used only during generation or verification, not by a product action.
open_points.default_guess: Registry reads the table directly whenever it validates a submitted form field.

open_points.subject: Model M31 — ProjectStatusConfirmation
open_points.text: The release: the project confirmation table the data provider holds.
open_points.question: Which product action reads ProjectStatusConfirmation: rendering a project card, beginning archive or erase confirmation, executing the confirmed change, or some combination of these?
options: The project-card read uses it to choose the offered confirmed action.
The archive and erase confirmation actions use it, but ordinary card reads do not.
Only release-generation or interface assembly reads it; no runtime product action does.
Both card rendering and confirmation processing read it.
open_points.default_guess: The owner-interface project-card read uses it to select the confirmation action, and confirmation processing validates against the same table.

open_points.subject: Model M32 — ImportFormFailureField
open_points.text: The release: the import form failure table the data provider holds.
open_points.question: Which import or form action reads ImportFormFailureField, and does it map failures while validating the uploaded import, while rendering the failure response, or only when assembling the release?
options: Import validation reads it when assigning each form failure to a mapping field.
Failure-response rendering reads it after validation reports a form field.
Both validation and response rendering read it.
It is build-time data and no runtime product action reads it.
open_points.default_guess: The import-validation action reads it when converting a form-field failure into the mapping field shown to the owner.

open_points.subject: Model M32 — ImportFormFailureField
open_points.text: One row for each form field the import checks.
open_points.question: Which form fields does the import check and therefore which FormField-to-MappingField rows exist, beyond the two examples given?
options: Only alias and customer kind have rows.
Every field accepted by the import form has a row.
Only fields whose displayed mapping-field name differs from their form-field name have rows.
A separately named provider table supplies a closed exhaustive row set.
open_points.default_guess: A named provider constant supplies one exhaustive row for every import form field that can produce a form failure.

open_points.subject: Model M33 — CustomerEligibilityRefusal
open_points.text: The release: the customer eligibility refusal table the data provider holds.
open_points.question: Which product actions read CustomerEligibilityRefusal when a project attempts to name a customer?
options: Project creation, project correction and import all read it.
Only project creation and correction read it; import has separate rules.
Only a shared customer-eligibility validator reads it, and product actions receive its resolved result.
It is build-time data and no runtime product action reads it.
open_points.default_guess: A shared validator reads it for every action that can newly link a project to a customer, including create, correction and import.

open_points.subject: Model M33 — CustomerEligibilityRefusal
open_points.text: A row of the customer eligibility refusal table: the kind of refusal a project's customer is refused with, by the customer's eligibility — an erased, restricted or ended customer (R0-16, R0-51, R0-57).
open_points.question: What RefusalKind value corresponds to each of erased, restricted and ended eligibility, and may two or all three eligibilities share one refusal kind?
options: Each eligibility has its own refusal kind.
All three map to one generic customer-ineligible refusal kind.
Some eligibilities share a refusal kind and others have distinct kinds.
The provider table is authoritative, but its exact exhaustive rows must be named here.
open_points.default_guess: Use a distinct refusal kind for erased, restricted and ended customers unless an explicitly named provider table declares shared values.

witness.initial: An active project-creation form names a restricted customer.
events: The owner submits the creation form.
Registry determines that the customer is restricted and consults the eligibility-refusal correspondence.
outcomes: The owner receives a refusal kind specific to restriction.
The owner receives a generic customer-ineligible refusal kind shared with erased or ended customers.
witness.observer: The owner and any contract consumer reading the refusal kind

open_points.subject: Model M34 — StoreCompanionStepSuffix
open_points.text: The release: the store companion table the data provider holds.
open_points.question: Which product or lifecycle action reads StoreCompanionStepSuffix, and at what lifecycle event is the table applied?
options: Discarding a newly created store reads it after a failed initialization or migration.
Normal shutdown reads it whenever Registry closes its store.
A deployment or maintenance tool reads it outside Registry.
It is build-time data and no runtime action reads it.
open_points.default_guess: Registry reads it only while discarding a newly created store after creation fails and must remove its companion files.

open_points.subject: Model M34 — StoreCompanionStepSuffix
open_points.text: A row of the store companion table: the suffix of the companion file a step of discarding a new store removes, by that step — the write-ahead log, the shared memory and the journal.
open_points.question: What exact suffix fact belongs to each discard step, and are the write-ahead-log, shared-memory and journal rows all present in every release?
options: The rows map the three steps to `-wal`, `-shm` and `-journal`, respectively.
The provider may choose different suffix values per release.
Only companions enabled by the selected store mode have rows.
The table contains all three rows, but another state defines their string values.
open_points.default_guess: The immutable release table contains all three rows mapped to `-wal`, `-shm` and `-journal`.

witness.initial: Creation of a new store has produced a write-ahead-log companion and then fails.
events: Registry begins discarding the new store.
The discard step reads the suffix associated with the write-ahead-log companion.
outcomes: It resolves the suffix to `-wal` and removes the companion file.
It resolves a different or absent suffix and leaves or targets a different file.
witness.observer: The owner or operator inspecting the store directory after the failed creation
